exclusions.A: The piano stood where it always had, at the far end from the stove.
exclusions.B: He fitted a new string from his case and tuned it to match the rest, at Rusk's pitch.
exclusions.C: Abel struck the low C, and the buzz came at once.
exclusions.E: Abel, listening from the back row, heard the low C ring true on the final chord.

WV10-P01.4.note: Abel strikes a piano key (the low C) to make it sound, so 'struck' means pressed.

exclusions.B: Here is the monster that sent you running to Mrs. Garvey.
exclusions.C: He coiled it and dropped it into her palm with a little bow.
exclusions.D: Abel, who had shared a desk with her at school forty years before, held up the broken string between two fingers.

WV10-P01.5.note: Calling a snapped string a 'monster' to be framed, delivered with a little bow to an old schoolmate, is gentle teasing that shows amusement; a pointed-rebuke reading (indignant) is not supported by the bow or the friendship.

exclusions.A: A raffle raised four thousand pounds across the town, and the money paid for the restoration
exclusions.B: When it closed in 1958, the council sold it off piece by piece, and the horses went to families across the valley who bought them for a few shillings each.
exclusions.D: the band organ, its painted front intact, needed only new bellows
exclusions.E: the council agreed in one evening that the carousel should stand on the common, so the letter went unsent.

WV10-P02.4.note: A raffle gathers money from people across the town, so 'raised' means collected, not increased an existing sum.

exclusions.A: Sure of her welcome, Nora told the Courier the grey would be home by Easter before writing to Hal, and he read it there first.
exclusions.B: The grey came home in June, after Nora drove out to the Brigg farm to apologise.
exclusions.C: When she did ask, his answer was two lines: she might have asked a man before announcing his property in the paper, and she could come and discuss it once she had learned some manners.
exclusions.D: That left the grey, which Hal Brigg's father had bought at the auction.

WV10-P02.5.note: Hal's curt rebuke about being announced in the paper before being asked, and Nora's need to apologise, show he is indignant; a dry/playful reading is undercut by the apology.

exclusions.A: In May a boardwalk opened, with lamps that switch off at ten, hours before the beetles stir
exclusions.B: Much had changed on the spit that year.
exclusions.C: the park had wanted them on all night, but the power bill ran to nine thousand dollars a year.
exclusions.E: Over the winter the park had put up a sand fence along the south end of the dune foot, beside the car park.

WV10-P03.4.note: A bill that 'ran to nine thousand dollars' amounted to that sum.

exclusions.B: Vell handed it back unsigned, with the 2013 pages clipped to the front, and told him to read them before he wrote a fourth.
exclusions.E: Arkin brought Vell a letter asking the park to take down the fence and switch off the lamps, the third such letter he had drafted that week, and asked her to sign it.

WV10-P03.5.note: Refusing the third letter that week and telling him to read the 2013 pages first reads literally as mild exasperation (irritated), but 'before he wrote a fourth' can be taken as dry teasing, which would support playful.
